action_plan.context: User side note 2026-09-12: the levels and obstacles need to present a cohesive challenge. Evidence already on hand: a shield-avoiding bot cleared 24/24 runs across L4-L9 (task 115 measurement), the Act 2 finale L6 fell in 4 hits to the bot where L1 took 9, and human L1 takes 10.5 hits on standard while human L6 heavy took 2 - so the curve is inverted for the player as well. SCOPE EXPANDED 2026-09-14 by the user, who asked for three things to be folded in here rather than filed separately - they are level-design vocabulary, which is what this gate exists to decide. (1) MOVEMENT ZONES: a region the player's hand is allowed to occupy on some levels. The stated flaw is that the player can currently flail wildly to win, and constraining where you may swing should promote deliberate, accurate play. NOTE THE PRECEDENT: a hand constraint was tried before - the `hand` dev knob capping px per frame - and the 2026-09-11 decision records it as having capped the skill ceiling while not fixing the tunneling it was for. A positional zone is a different constraint (where, not how fast) and plausibly increases skill expression rather than capping it, but the design should engage with that history rather than rediscover it. Also connects to the task 149 finding that shield placement dominated shield tier: if where the player can be is the strongest lever, a zone controls it directly instead of regulating it downstream. (2) BLADE/RAZOR OBSTACLE: cuts the tail and fails the level. Feasible specifically because of the task 124 link-level CCD work, which took rope link crossings from 5-7.5% to under 1% - without accurate rope collision a blade would kill through phantom contacts the renderer never drew. Implementation likely leans on detachRope. (3) GENERAL REORGANISATION of the levels. CROSS-CUTTING DECISION THIS GATE SHOULD SETTLE ONCE: the game currently has no way to lose, only to score badly. The blade introduces failure, and so does task 151's alternate-win mode, so the question is arriving from two directions and should be decided deliberately rather than twice. action_plan.done_when: The rat cannot leave the playable area at any speed reached in normal play, verified by a rig that drives it hard at each boundary and asserts it stays inside.
action_plan.context: Reported by the user 2026-09-16 - the rat occasionally gets caught off screen or beyond the boundary. Two independent causes, both structural. (1) There is NO CEILING: physics init creates only groundBody, leftWall and rightWall, so nothing bounds the top. Once outside, the rat would have to tunnel back to return, which matches 'caught'. Cheapest likely fix is much thicker walls plus a ceiling, which costs nothing per step and changes no game feel; extending the rope's sweep to the rat is the alternative but would touch the body that carries the damage. THE GUARD IS STRUCTURAL, NOT BEHAVIOURAL, and that was earned: the first version whipped the hand at the boundaries and PASSED with the ceiling deliberately removed, because the escape took 90 iterations to reproduce and the check ran 80. decisions.decision: Tail-attachment rebalance settled after 4 rounds of playtesting. Final values — standard rat: mass 1.0→4.5, frictionAir 0.005→0.025, restitution 0.35→0.05; heavy rat: mass 3.5→11.5, frictionAir 0.003→0.015, restitution 0.1→0.02; constraint stiffness 0.65→0.35
decisions.rationale: The first two tuning passes (mass/frictionAir increases, stiffness decreases) weren't enough — user reported no major difference. The decisive change was reversing frictionAir direction to a sharp ~5x increase (faster momentum decay, more effort to reach top speed) and dropping rat restitution near zero (less bounce, more hit-and-slide). Accepted as good for now. Caveat: Matter.js resolves collision restitution as max(rat, target), so steel targets (restitution 0.55 in target.js) will still bounce regardless of the rat's value — a target.js follow-up if that surfaces during task 45's full playthrough.

decisions.decision: Heavier impact feedback (supersedes #48, expanded to include rat body-wear): extend particles.js with a rotating 'chunk' shape; on every HP-damage hit, fire three damage-scaled bursts (red blood splash, target-material chunk debris via material.crackedColor, rat-fur chunk debris via a new variant color); reuse the already-generated-but-unrendered yoyo.plugin.crackPattern to draw scuff marks on the rat's body via drawCracks(), plus an HP-based body color blend toward a new worn tone
decisions.rationale: Builds entirely on existing systems — particles.js's emit/update/draw loop, target.js's crackedColor palette, and main.js's dormant per-hit crackPattern generation for the rat body — so no new physics bodies or rendering pipelines are needed. This keeps the change low-risk and avoids the perf cost of spawning Matter.js fragments on every combo hit (a physics-debris approach was considered and rejected for that reason). The new 'chunk' particle shape gives debris a distinct angular silhouette from the round blood splashes.

decisions.decision: Four-part tuning/feature round (tasks 63-74), surfaced during task 45's playthrough: (1) recalibrate speed meter + damage formula — pushMaxSpeed ×1.25 (standard 600→750, heavy 500→625) and DAMAGE_SCALE 1200→2000, with the shake-threshold and damageIntensity-saturation constants rescaled ×0.6 to match — so the realistic top swing speed reads as 60% on the meter and 1-hit shatters require near-max effort/combo; (2) shape variety — convert 3 rectangle targets (levels 1, 3, 7) to circles; (3) a new moving-target mechanic — static bodies repositioned via Body.setPosition along a sine wave, driven by a `movement: { axis, range, period }` level schema field, applied to levels 6 and 9; (4) replace the 4 geometric giblet fragment shapes with organic jittered-radius 'flesh chunk' blobs; (5) shorten/soften the rat's swing trail by activating the previously-dormant per-variant trailLength field (20/12 vs the global cap of 30) and lowering the trail's alpha multiplier
decisions.rationale: Recalibration keeps the meter/damage relationship internally consistent (pushMaxSpeed and DAMAGE_SCALE scaled by inverse factors) while raising the skill ceiling, rather than just rescaling the HUD. Moving targets reuse static bodies + Body.setPosition so collision/damage formulas need no changes — a dynamic-body approach was rejected as unnecessary complexity. Giblet blobs and trail tone-down both activate/reuse existing per-fragment and per-variant data rather than adding new state, consistent with this project's preference for repurposing dormant fields.

decisions.decision: Corrected the task-63 damage recalibration: DAMAGE_SCALE 2000→200 (a 10x cut), with damageIntensity's saturation point (24→240) and the screen-shake damage threshold (12→120, shakeIntensity divisor 8→80) scaled by the same factor to preserve their relative tuning; CLAUDE.md's HP system and Impact feedback bullets updated, and the now-disproven '~450px/60%=realistic ceiling' claim removed pending real swing-speed data.
decisions.rationale: Playtesting the tasks 63-74 round found Level 1 took 30-40 hits to clear versus the ~2-3 hits the task-63 calibration targeted — the underlying assumption (real swings reach ~60% of the new 750 pushMaxSpeed, i.e. ~450 px/step) was wrong; actual swings land far slower. Deliberately NOT part of this work: any change to gameplay constants (DAMAGE_SCALE, pushMaxSpeed, thresholds) — this measures, and tuning is a separate decision once numbers exist. Standing caveat: a bot's swing profile is not a human's, so bot data is valid for regression detection and relative A/B of constants, while absolute calibration must rest on human-run telemetry — calibrating constants on bot swings would repeat the L0097 unmeasured-premise error that produced the 30-40-hit Level 1.

Which way to resolve the target question is a design fork (indestructible-by-design with the misleading Brittle label removed, vs. targets becoming breakable) that changes the core loop, so it goes through the design gate rather than being patched.

decisions.decision: MEASURED human swing range (standard variant), replacing the assumption that has driven every balance decision to date. Free-swing calibration: peak 1146, p90 374, p50 177. In play across 9 runs (L2-L9): per-run peak p50 310 / max 400, sustained p50 109 (range 32-139), hits to clear min 4 / p50 6 / max 12, time to clear p50 9.5s, 35% of 66 hits glancing (angleFactor < 0.55).
decisions.rationale: The premise behind the task 63-75 miscalibration was that real swings reach ~60% of pushMaxSpeed (=450 for standard). Measurement shows that is wrong in both directions depending on what is measured: sustained in-play speed is 109, only 14.5% of pushMaxSpeed, while a free swing peaks at 1146, i.e. 153% OF the supposed maximum. pushMaxSpeed=750 is therefore not a ceiling at all, yet in actual play peaks top out near 400 (53%), so the speed meter never fills past about half while playing - it is normalised against a speed only reachable when not playing. Bot comparison: bot peak speed (p50 ~320) tracks human peaks (310) closely, but bot SUSTAINED speed (p50 ~51) is less than half the human 109, and since damage scales with speed squared the bot understates human damage per typical hit by roughly 4.5x. Level-by-level the bot is not a human proxy at all - it cleared L6 in 4 hits/2.4s where the human needed 7 hits/10.6s, and needed 9 hits on L1 where the human cleared L2 in 4. Confirms bot data is usable for regression detection and peak-speed comparison, not for difficulty or absolute tuning. NOT YET MEASURED: the heavy variant (pushMaxSpeed 625) has no calibration run, and no human run exists for L1.

decisions.decision: Segmented rope design (tasks 116-121): replace the single tail Constraint with a Matter chain of ~10 collidable bodies; TRUE WRAP (the rope may coil a bumper and shorten the effective radius) with a player-initiated yank to unwind; the rat gains collision with ground and walls. Built behind ?dev=1&rope=N so the batch can A/B it at identical seeds, flag removed on merge.
decisions.rationale: Wrap must emerge from real collision solving, so a hand-rolled Verlet rope was ruled out and the approach collapsed to a Matter body chain - the remaining variable is segment count and stiffness, which the batch runner can measure rather than guess. User chose true wrap over contact-drag-only, player-initiated release over auto-recovery or retry, and full rat/world collision. A collision-category cleanup is a hard prerequisite: ground and walls never set a collisionFilter and so inherited Matter default 0x0001, the same bit the rat uses, making it impossible for rope to collide with world geometry without colliding with the rat. The yank is deliberately energy-neutral (impulse toward the pivot plus tangential damping, on a cooldown) because an accelerating yank would become the dominant strategy; that risk is checked by measurement - a yank-spam batch must show no advantage - rather than by judgement.

decisions.decision: Rope parameters set by sweep: 10 segments, per-segment mass 5% of rat mass, engine.constraintIterations 48 while a rope is attached (Matter default 2 restored for the un-roped path). Circles of radius 3.5, stiffness 1.0, zero constraint damping, frictionAir 0.0005.
decisions.rationale: Segment mass is the dominant term and the naive value was badly wrong. At 1-2% of rat mass the rope swallowed the swing entirely - peak speed collapsed from ~320 to 40 and the bot never cleared - because a near-massless chain cannot pull a body 100x heavier through Matter sequential solver. Raising constraintIterations helps (2% mass: 102 at 20 iters, 138 at 40, 161 at 60) but does not converge to usable, so a genuinely light rope is not achievable here. At 25% per segment the rope matches the no-rope baseline but totals 2.5x the rat mass and reads as a chain rather than a tail. 5% with 40-60 iterations clears 100% of runs at median peak 208-240 against a 315 baseline, i.e. a 25-30% momentum cost, which is the hindrance the rope exists to create. Frame p95 stays 16.7ms even at 60 iterations, so iteration count is not a perf constraint. Matter default 2 constraint iterations also let the 10-link chain stretch ~30% under the rat weight, lengthening the effective pendulum from 130 to 171px; at 48 iterations the span is 131.

decisions.decision: Rope vs no-rope measured across all 9 levels and both variants (108 runs, identical seeds, fixed timestep). Result: the rope makes the game EASIER, not harder - median hits to clear 5 -> 3 (-40%), time to clear 4.1s -> 2.7s (-33%) - despite cutting peak speed 337 -> 237 (-30%). DAMAGE_SCALE and every other gameplay constant left unchanged.
decisions.rationale: The mechanism is the opposite of the intent and only measurement would have found it. Rope mass acts as a flywheel: peak speed falls 30% but SUSTAINED speed rises 23% (p50 50.1 -> 61.5) and glancing hits fall 36% (35.5% -> 22.8%). Since damage scales with speed squared and with angleFactor, a steady clean swing out-damages a peaky sloppy one, so fewer hits are needed. Momentum IS hindered as the feature intended - peak is down 30% - but peak is not what governs difficulty here. No constant was retuned because the rope moves bot median hits to clear to 3, inside the 3-4 design target, where no-rope sat at 5; the honest next step is a human re-calibration (task 121), not tuning against bot numbers. SOFT-LOCK FOUND: Level 8 with rope and no yank fails 6/6 with ZERO contacts and ZERO hits - the rope tangles slack and the bot cannot build a swing at all, so it never reaches the target. With a yank every 1.2s it clears 3/3. The yank is therefore load-bearing rather than a convenience, which retrospectively validates choosing player-initiated release over auto-recovery - but the game never tells the player that clicking yanks, so discoverability is now a real gap. Rope contacts are highest on the Act 2 shield levels L4 (80) and L6 (76).

decisions.decision: Rope tunneling root-caused to unbounded hand speed, not gravity or rope parameters. Hand rate limit and physics sub-stepping added as dev-tunable knobs (?dev=1&hand=N&subs=N) with defaults unchanged; the user will choose values by feel before they become defaults.
decisions.rationale: updatePivot wrote the pointer position directly into constraint.pointA, so the hand could teleport 234px in one frame (p50 10.6, p90 107.5) and whip the rat to a 249px/step peak against 44px bumpers. Matter has no continuous collision detection, and with p50 rat speed at 65px/step more than half of all steps already exceed a bumper diameter, so this was routine rather than a rare peak. Sub-stepping alone is not a fix: contact counts never plateau (48/39/100/157/266/288/843 at 1/2/4/8/12/16/24 sub-steps) because even 24 sub-steps leaves ~35px per sub-step, and each level is also a large difficulty change. Reducing gravity was rejected as the mechanism because the player drives the pivot directly, so player-driven speed is not bounded by gravity at all - the game would become floaty without fixing the cause. Capping the hand bounds the system where the energy actually enters. Chosen as a feel decision rather than a measured one because it caps the skill ceiling: today whipping the mouse faster is always better, which is why the human free-swing calibration hit 1146 while in-play sustained sat at 109. A correction worth recording: an earlier probe comparing body velocity against position delta was tautological, since Matter defines velocity AS the position delta, so it could not have distinguished real motion from solver correction as claimed.

decisions.decision: Rope tunneling fixed with manual continuous collision detection for rope segments only (Matter.Query.ray sweep plus an 8-step binary search for the last free point), default on. The hand cap, sub-stepping and segment speed clamp remain as dev knobs but are NOT the fix and stay at their original defaults.
decisions.rationale: No parameter could fix this. Rope segments whip to 432 px/step against 44px bumpers; sub-stepping made it marginally worse (26.3% to 30.5% over-44 from 4 to 8 sub-steps) because better constraint solving stiffens the rope; a velocity clamp cannot bound displacement because the constraint solver repositions bodies directly, independent of velocity. Matter 0.19 ships no CCD and this game sits in the regime where discrete collision fails. Sweeping is contained to the rope because the rat is large and carries the damage, so the rat speed, the hand and the game feel are untouched - unlike the hand cap, which capped the skill ceiling AND still left 26% of samples tunneling. Cost is negligible because segments moving less than their own radius are skipped, which is most of them.

decisions.decision: Rope collision strengthened with a second CCD pass at link level plus segment radius 5.0. Link crossings fall from 5-7.5% to under 1% and segment penetration stays at zero.
decisions.rationale: Per-segment sweeping fixed body penetration but not the visible clipping, because the rope is a chain of circles separated by 6px gaps and the line between two segments can cut an obstacle while neither endpoint is inside it. Closing the gap geometrically was measured and is insufficient on its own: 10 segments at radius 6.5 (zero gap) reached 2.74%, and adding segments made things WORSE (14 -> 3.11%, 20 -> 4.19%) because more links mean a floppier rope that whips harder. The link pass uses the same rewind-toward-previous-position trick as the segment sweep, so it is shape-agnostic and works for circles and rectangles alike, and it skips links that were already crossing before the step since rewinding those would freeze the rope against the obstacle. Radius 5.0 measured best of 3.5/5.0/6.5 with the link pass active.

decisions.decision: Merged branch swinging/feat/segmented-rope into main (with its stacked parents swinging/feat/playtest-bot-telemetry and swinging/feat/realistic-giblets, 20 commits)

Human calibration on the rope build. Standard: free-swing p50 133.6, p90 280.4, peak 719.6. Heavy: p50 113.1, p90 227.1, peak 784.3. Heavy pushMaxSpeed raised 625 -> 785 to match its measured ceiling; standard left at 750. DAMAGE_SCALE deliberately NOT changed.
decisions.rationale: The rope costs real momentum, now measured on a human rather than the bot: against the 2026-09-06 pre-rope calibration, standard free-swing peak fell 1146 -> 719.6 (-37%), p90 374 -> 280.4 (-25%) and p50 177 -> 133.6 (-25%). That is the hindrance the rope was built for. It also fixed the speed meter almost by accident: standard now peaks at 96% of its pushMaxSpeed where it previously hit 153% and saturated, so the meter is correctly scaled for the first time. Heavy still overshot at 125%, so its value was raised to its measured 784 - safe because pushMaxSpeed is a presentation knob with exactly one use (normalising the meter and the whoosh in main.js:420) and never enters the damage formula, which keeps balance and presentation knobs orthogonal per L0120. DAMAGE_SCALE stays at 200 because the data does not yet support a change: the only rope-build in-play runs are two Level 7 clears at 7 and 8 hits, and Level 1 - the level the 3-4 hit target was actually written against - has no rope-build run at all. Changing a damage constant on two runs of the wrong level would repeat the reasoning-from-insufficient-data error this whole effort exists to prevent.

decisions.decision: Level 1 human runs close task 127. Standard median 10.5 hits, heavy median 5 - both miss the documented 3-4 hit target, standard by about 3x. Two earlier claims corrected: heavy does NOT swing slower in play, and the bot is NOT a good proxy for human difficulty.
decisions.rationale: Measured on the level the 3-4 target was actually written against. Standard: 11/17/10/6 hits, median 10.5, 7.1s, scoring the 200 floor every time, 31% glancing. Heavy: 4/5/5/5, median 5, 3.5s, score 1000, 15% glancing. CORRECTION 1 - I previously said heavy swings ~15% slower, from free-swing calibration (p50 113 vs 134). In play the two are identical (114.1 vs 114.4), so the trade-off justifying heavy 2.2x impactMultiplier does not exist where it matters; observed damage per hit is 18.3 vs 7.7, a clean 2.4x with nothing offsetting it. CORRECTION 2 - I noted last turn that the bot appeared to track human numbers. On L1 it does not: bot standard 6 vs human 10.5, bot heavy 2 vs human 5, so the bot is roughly twice as effective as the player and the earlier agreement on L4 was coincidence. The standing caveat that bot data is for regression and relative comparison, not absolute difficulty, holds. DAMAGE_SCALE still not changed: tripling damage to bring standard to target would drop heavy to ~2 hits, so the variant imbalance (task 126) has to be resolved first or any global tuning bakes it in.

decisions.decision: Merged branch swinging/fix/speed-meter-calibration into main

Task 126 resolved by design gate: the rat variants become an explicit difficulty selector with par-relative scoring. Heavy impactMultiplier 2.2 -> 1.4, DAMAGE_SCALE 200 -> 80, per-variant parHits (standard 5, heavy 3), calcPushScore gains a parHits parameter, and the picker gets Hard/Easy labels. No score tax.
decisions.rationale: The game has no cost axis at all: the rat's only resource is HP and spending HP is winning, so impactMultiplier is one-sided and any variant carrying more of it is permanently strictly better (L0250). Reading the code settled what the task description left open - main.js:247 ends the level when the rat's own HP hits 0 and calcPushScore(hitCount) is the only scored term, so targets are anvils and hits are the sole metric. Two findings redirected the fix. First, calcPushScore has a live gradient only from 1 to 6 hits and standard's measured median of 10.5 sits four hits past the end of it, so a standard player improving 17 -> 11 hits sees no score change at all; that unscorable band, not the variant gap, is the substance of task 129, and no score multiplier addresses it. Second, the hard/easy axis is already physically real and shipped: radius 22 vs 18 produces 15% vs 31% glancing hits through angleFactor, which is a shaped cost rather than a described one (L0373). So the design keeps the precision gap as the difficulty axis, closes the unjustified raw-damage gap on top of it, and pulls both variants inside the live scoring range. Par-relative scoring was chosen over the flat score multiplier sketched in the earlier options because the 500-per-hit curve is steep enough that any sane multiplier has to be re-derived every time a hit count moves; scoring each variant against its own par lets both reach 3000 by mastery, makes standard's harder par pay more for the same absolute feat, and - with parHits defaulting to 1 - leaves the existing function behaviour and all 6 scoring tests untouched. REJECTED: per-material variant affinity (a real strategic choice, but a larger new mechanic); equalising power and differentiating on feel alone (removes strategy); relabel-plus-multiplier only (3 lines, but leaves 129 unfixed on the 200 floor). ACCEPTED CONSEQUENCES: cross-variant high scores stop being directly comparable, and saved scores earned on the old scale will be beaten easily - no migration for a single-player local game. COUPLING CHECK (L0169): three feedback constants read raw damage magnitude - damageIntensity /240, shakeIntensity /80, and hitStopTimer derived from the former - so their divisors scale by the same 2.5 (to 96 and 32) to hold felt output constant and keep hit count the only variable this change introduces (L0227). Noted while checking: damageIntensity currently peaks at 0.08 of its range, so burst scaling and hit-stop are effectively dormant at today's damage values - logged as its own task rather than fixed by accident.

decisions.decision: Add a READY state between PICKER and SWINGING: the rat starts slumped on the ground with its tail stretched out beside it, and the player grabs the tail tip to begin play. The lift is done by the game's own physics - grabbing creates the pivot constraint at the pointer, and raising the hand pulls the rope taut and hauls the rat up - rather than by an animation or a snap.
decisions.rationale: The reported glitch on entering a level was diagnosed rather than assumed: the rat spawns motionless at pivot + pushStringLength (L1: pivot y 310, rat y 440) and nothing moves until the first pointermove over the canvas, at which point the pivot TELEPORTS from the level-defined position to wherever the cursor happens to be - usually still over the Launch button - and whips the rat. A tail grab fixes this by construction, because the pointer IS the grab point, so there is no jump left to make. Chosen over two alternatives: a scripted lift tween (an input-locked animation is the same class of thing that reads as glitchy, and it re-creates in code what gravity already does) and an instant snap on grab (cheapest, but it relocates the teleport to the moment of the grab rather than removing it). The physics lift also turned out to be the LEAST code: attachRope already builds the segment chain, the segment-to-segment constraints and the rat link as separate blocks, with the pivot anchor (stringConstraint, pointA -> ropeBodies[0]) as one distinct block, so deferring that single block is the whole feature and ropeBodies[0] becomes the free tail tip that serves as the grab target. TWO CONSTRAINTS BUILT IN RATHER THAN BOLTED ON: (1) the grab is now mandatory, and an untaught mandatory affordance is a hard stop - the game cannot start at all if the player does not find it - which is L0364 logged from this very project when the yank quietly became load-bearing while still untaught; hence a prompt, a pulsing tip highlight, and a hit radius sized for touch rather than for the 5px segment body. (2) the dev rigs drive beginRun() directly (gate.mjs, run-batch.mjs, ab.mjs), so beginRun auto-grabs and no rig needs special-casing. BLOCKER FOUND DURING DESIGN: the physics floor and the drawn floor do not line up - groundBody's top surface is at y 620, the canvas bottom edge, while drawGround paints its surface line at y 580. Fragments already sink 40px into the dirt and paintSplat hides it by drawing decals at the visual line regardless of where the body actually is. A rat posed on the ground would be almost entirely buried, so aligning the ground is a required part of this change, not a bonus; it also fixes the pre-existing fragment sink. Levels are unaffected because the lowest target sits around y 459. ACCEPTED CONSEQUENCE: every level now opens with hauling the rat up, so bot baselines shift and task 133's human measurement must wait until this lands, or the rebalance gets measured twice.

decisions.decision: Tail-grab pickup accepted on feel. User played the served build and confirmed the new pick-up reads better than the old immediate start.
decisions.rationale: The feature existed to fix a perceptual complaint - entering a level 'seems glitchy' - so perceptual acceptance is the real gate and green tests could never have supplied it (same standard as task 98). Mechanical verification was already in place: 74/74 vitest, 92/92 gate across five consecutive runs, and committed screenshots of READY, the grab and the lift. NOT a substitute for task 133: an impression of the rebalance is not the recorded per-variant hit counts that 126 and 129 need.

decisions.decision: Measured the rebalance on 10 human L1 runs. Par-relative scoring is validated exactly, task 129 is closed, but the difficulty-selector premise is refuted and the variant imbalance has inverted rather than resolved.
decisions.rationale: Brown Rat/standard (par 5): 2/4500, 4/3500, 3/4000, 4/3500, 4/3500 - mean 3.4 hits, median 4, range 2-4, mean score 3800. Sewer Rat/heavy (par 3): 3/3000, 3/3000, 2/3500, 4/2500, 3/3000 - mean 3.0 hits, median 3, range 2-4, mean score 3000. THREE CONCLUSIONS. (1) VALIDATED: all 10 observed scores match calcPushScore(hits, parHits) to the point, so the implementation is correct against real play. (2) 129 CLOSED: standard L1 is median 4 hits against the 3-4 target, down from 10.5, and never touches the 200 floor - lowest score 3500. (3) 126 NOT CLOSED, AND INVERTED: standard now out-scores heavy 3800 to 3000. The prediction was wrong in a direction worth recording - standard was extrapolated to 5.2 hits from median damage-per-hit of 7.7 x 2.5, but plays at 3.4, meaning real damage per hit is nearer 29 than 19. The extrapolation failed because damage-per-hit is NOT independent of hit count: the old 10.5-hit runs were padded with weak and glancing contacts that drag the median down, and when a run only needs 3 hits those weak hits never happen. Hits-to-kill cannot be projected from a median damage sample taken at a different hit count. The knock-on is that standard's par of 5 was set from that bad prediction and is 1.6 hits too generous, handing it +800 every run, while heavy's par of 3 matches its measured 3.0. Correcting standard to par 4 centres both variants on 3000 - but it also makes explicit that the two rats now play the same, so the Hard/Easy framing has no measured difficulty behind it.

decisions.decision: Standard parHits corrected 5 -> 4 to its measured L1 median. The Hard/Easy framing is NOT settled: it is deferred until one late Act 3 level is measured, because L1 is the worst place in the game to look for a difficulty gap.
decisions.rationale: Par 5 came from an extrapolation of 5.2 hits; standard plays at 3.4 with a median of 4, so the old par handed it +800 a run and inverted the very imbalance the rebalance was meant to fix. Par 4 matches the median and brings the residual advantage down from +800 to +300, which is inside the noise at n=5. Deliberately NOT over-fitted to the 3.4 mean: par 3 would swing standard to -200 instead, and with five runs the median is the more defensible read. The framing question is separate and genuinely open. The L1 measurement says the two rats are indistinguishable (3.4 vs 3.0 mean hits), but L1 is the shortest level in the game and a 2-4 hit band has nowhere to put a gap, so concluding the variants are identical from it would be overreaching. Acts 2-3 have shields, bumpers and more targets, giving longer runs in which the precision difference (31% vs 15% glancing) has room to express itself - or to be ruled out properly. Tests survived this retune untouched because they assert against RAT_VARIANTS.parHits rather than the literals (L0352), which is exactly the case that learning was written for.

decisions.decision: 29 telemetry-captured human runs across L2-L9 settle task 143 (no precision difference - it is inverted) and expose a regression: DAMAGE_SCALE 80 makes Acts 2-3 trivial, with 34% one-hit clears. Recommend NOT merging either branch until damage is re-pitched across levels.
decisions.rationale: TASK 143 ANSWERED NO. Standard glances 19.3% of contacts, heavy 28.6% - the reverse of the 31% vs 15% the difficulty-selector design was built on. Heavy also clears L8 in a median 1.5 hits to standard's 3.0 and out-damages it 44.3 to 31.7 p50, a ratio of 1.40 matching impactMultiplier exactly. There is no precision cost to trade against the multiplier, so the Hard/Easy framing has no support and the labels should come off. The original 31/15 split was measured on the PRE-rebalance build at L1, where runs were 10.5 hits long and glancing had room to register; at 1-2 hits per run it barely can. MY ERROR, AND THE BIGGER FINDING: DAMAGE_SCALE 200 -> 80 was validated on Level 1 alone - the shortest level in the game - and is badly wrong everywhere else. Acts 2-3 now clear in a median of 2 hits with 34% one-hit clears, and a single recorded L9 hit dealt 279.78 damage to a 100 HP rat. A global divisor cannot fix this, because the spread is across levels rather than a constant offset: glass yoyoDamage 0.6 against steel 1.6 is already 2.67x, and Act 3 swing speeds are far higher, which speed-squared amplifies to a 10x-plus swing in damage per hit between L1 and L9. Raising DAMAGE_SCALE to fix Act 3 would push L1 back off the 3-4 hit target that task 129 just met. This needs a design pass over per-level or per-material damage, not another constant nudge, and it should block the merge - shipping this would make the campaign finale a one-hit level.

decisions.decision: Task 144 implemented: per-hit HP damage capped at 40% of RAT_MAX_HP, material yoyoDamage spread narrowed 0.6/1.0/1.6 -> 0.85/1.0/1.15, and feedback split off to read the raw uncapped value. DAMAGE_SCALE deliberately left at 80.
decisions.rationale: The measurement reframed the task. Over 61 human hits the medians were already correct - p50 41 against a 100 HP rat is a 2-3 hit pace - but p75 was 113 and the max 426, so 34% of individual hits ended a level outright. That is a tail problem, not a scale problem, and the answer is a bound rather than a rescale (L0250: a knob that only ever helps needs an explicit bound). Simulation over the observed hits chose the numbers rather than taste (L0390): a 40% cap puts every level in a 3-5 hit band with zero one-shots, where 50% leaves L4/L5 at 2 and 34% pushes L2/L3 to 5. DAMAGE_SCALE STAYS AT 80 because raising it makes things worse, not better - at 145 the inter-level range widens to 3-8 and at 200 to 3-11, since the cap pins high-damage levels at 3 while low-damage ones stretch out. THE MATERIAL HALF: yoyoDamage narrowed because steel one-shot on 60% of hits against glass's 23%, which made steel strictly better and inverted the difficulty curve. But rebalancing yoyoDamage ALONE cannot fix one-shots - flattening only moves 34% to 26%, inverting is worse at 33% and pushes max damage to 803, and the only scheme that works is an aggressive uniform cut, which is DAMAGE_SCALE renamed (L0409). So the spread fixes the inversion and the cap fixes the tail; they are complementary, not alternatives. THE FEEDBACK SPLIT is what makes the cap safe: HP subtracts the clamped value while shake, hit-stop, the particle burst and the hit sound all read rawDamage, so the cap bounds how the game plays without changing how a big hit looks - and the three feedback constants stay aimed at the raw series they were tuned against, avoiding the re-derivation that I inverted earlier in this session. FOUND ALONG THE WAY: materials are almost entirely decorative. evaluateImpact computes a SHATTER/CRACK/SURVIVE outcome that main.js:195 destructures and never uses, and removeTarget is called only for shields, so strength, crackThreshold and hardnessFactor affect nothing. yoyoDamage is the only mechanical material field, which is why C could not create a trade-off on its own - materials have no cost dimension, the same wall task 126 hit.

decisions.decision: Task 144 validated on 88 human runs and closed. The damage cap and narrowed material spread hit every target. Task 126 also closes: the rats are a feel choice, not a difficulty choice.
decisions.rationale: 88 post-cap human runs across all 9 levels and both variants: median 4 hits, range 3-7, ZERO one-hit clears against 34% before, every level's median inside the 3-5 target band, and the difficulty curve rising rather than inverted (Act 1 mean 3.60, Act 2 3.68, Act 3 3.81). Applied damage never exceeded 40 while raw damage reached 1381 - the cap absorbed the tail on 86 of 88 runs. TASK 126 SETTLED on the same data: glancing is 19.4% standard against 20.3% heavy, so the precision axis the difficulty-selector design rested on does not exist at any sample size we now have - the original 31% vs 15% was an artifact of the pre-rebalance build, where 10-hit runs gave glancing room to register. Heavy clears marginally faster at mean 3.55 against 3.91 but scores no better, because each variant is measured against its own par. So the honest answer to 'what is each rat FOR' is appearance, sound and handling - task 145 removes the Hard/Easy labels. SHIELDS, raised by the user and confirmed by telemetry: 8 of 106 contacts break, and the breakSpeed 180 tier was never broken in 36 contacts against a maximum recorded contact speed of 171.5. That threshold is not difficult, it is unreachable, and it is almost certainly rope fallout - the rope cost 25-37% of swing speed after those numbers were set. Logged as task 148 with a design gate, since tiering shields is a level-design vocabulary change and not a constant nudge.

decisions.decision: Picker labels rewritten to describe appearance only - 'Lean & scrappy' and 'Bulky & messy'. Task 145 closes and with it the last item blocking the merge.
decisions.rationale: Reverting to the original 'Quick & nimble' / 'Heavy & mean' was rejected: it would have swapped one false claim for another, since both rats clock the same in-play speed and heavy clears marginally faster, so standard was never the quick one. The new copy names only what a player can actually observe - size, the giblet spread on shatter via blastBonus, and trail length. The docs now carry the refutation itself rather than just the conclusion, because the failure mode is likely to recur: a plausible-sounding axis (bigger radius means cleaner hits means an easier rat) was asserted at 31% vs 15%, built into a whole design, and measured back at 19.4% vs 20.3%. The blockquote for adding a new variant tells the next author to measure whatever axis they think they have added before labelling it.

decisions.decision: Shields are authored by named tier (light 45 / medium 70 / heavy 95), replacing raw breakSpeed. The tier supplies both the break speed and the material it renders in, so the cost is legible before the player swings.
decisions.rationale: The old thresholds were set from the wrong distribution. Over 106 human contacts the speed a player actually ARRIVES with at a shield is p25 38, p50 50, p75 61, max 151 - far below free-swing peaks of ~720, because shield placement constrains the approach. The 100 and 180 thresholds therefore sat at 2x and 3.6x median arrival: 100 broke in 33% of runs and 180 in 0 of 13, so a whole tier displayed 'TOO SLOW!' and could never open. The rope almost certainly caused it, costing 25-37% of swing speed after those numbers were set. Tiers are derived from the measured first-contact distribution and projected at ~5 attempts per encounter (the ratio that fits 8% per-contact against 33% per-run), giving roughly 99% / 74% / 44% per-run success. Chosen over two alternatives: tier driving strength only, which leaves the tier invisible and therefore unable to guide anyone, and bespoke shield rendering, which buys clarity the existing material palette already carries. TWO GUARDS ADDED so this cannot recur - tiers must rise monotonically, and every tier must sit below MAX_OBSERVED_CONTACT_SPEED (150.8), which is the assertion that would have caught the 180 tier the day it was written (L0379). resolveShieldTier throws on an unknown tier rather than defaulting, since a silent default means breakSpeed 0 and a shield that shatters on contact - a failure that would look like success. CAUGHT BY SCREENSHOT, NOT BY TESTS: the first implementation rendered every shield the same hardcoded pale blue, so a wood and a steel shield were indistinguishable and the tier - the entire point of the feature - was invisible. Shields now take their tier's colour. This is the second time this session that a perceptual check found something a green suite could not.

decisions.decision: Shield tiers validated on 31 human runs and closed. Every tier now opens - the 0% tier is gone - though medium and heavy are barely separated in practice.
decisions.rationale: Per-run break rates by tier over 31 shield-bearing runs: light 82% (9 of 11 runs, 56% of 16 contacts), medium 61% (14 of 23 runs, 30% of 47 contacts), heavy 57% (4 of 7 runs, 40% of 10 contacts). NO TIER AT 0% - every tier opened, which was the defect. Projections were 99/74/44, so light and medium came in below and heavy above. Pacing was undisturbed: shield levels sit at median 3-4 hits, inside the band the damage cap established, so tiering did not disturb the balance work underneath it. THE FINDING WORTH CARRYING FORWARD is why medium and heavy came out nearly equal. Players arrive at heavy shields substantially faster - contact speed p50 72.0 at heavy against 53.1 at medium - and that 36% arrival gap almost exactly cancels the 36% threshold gap between 70 and 95. So a tier's difficulty is a function of placement as much as of its number, which is precisely the guidance lever the user asked for but also means the tier table alone cannot deliver a clean difficulty grade. Separating them would need a wider threshold gap (heavy contacts reached 120.6, so ~110 stays reachable) or deliberate placement, and heavy has only 7 runs behind it, so that is a change to make on more data rather than on this sample. ALSO NOTED: a light-tier contact reached 156.9, above the MAX_OBSERVED_CONTACT_SPEED of 150.8 the reachability guard uses. No tier is near that ceiling so nothing fails, but the constant is now stale by 6 px/step and should be refreshed when it is next touched.

decisions.decision: Merged branch swinging/feat/shield-tiers into main, carrying its three stacked parents (variant-difficulty-rebalance, tail-grab-pickup, damage-cap-material-spread) - 26 commits.

decisions.decision: Task 147 answered in two halves. For the campaign: materials are intentionally cosmetic plus one damage dial, and six dead fields plus evaluateImpact are removed. Destructible targets move to a NEW alternate-win level type, designed and deferred rather than retrofitted into the nine tuned levels.
decisions.rationale: 147 and 113 turned out to be the same discovery from opposite directions - 113 filed it on 2026-09-06 as 'wire up the outcome computed at physics.js:84 and discarded at main.js:166' (line numbers since drifted to 135 and 195), and 144's design re-found the dead code without noticing the existing item. THE CAMPAIGN HALF: an audit found no reader for strength, crackThreshold, hardnessFactor, density, fragmentCount or fragmentSpread. hardnessFactor was worse than unused - it still held 0.6/1.0/1.6, the pre-rebalance yoyoDamage values, so a stale copy of a live dial sat next to the real one. evaluateImpact was removed with them, and deliberately NOT kept as a seed for the future mode: its impulse = speed x mass x impactMultiplier formula gives heavy 3.58x standard at identical speed because it folds in mass, which is inert everywhere else since the player drives the pivot; measured, standard could not shatter steel in 25 hits while heavy managed 23%. Keeping it would have invited wiring up a model already known to re-create the imbalance task 126 removed. THE FEATURE HALF, deferred: the user reframed destructible targets as a separate level type with an INVERTED win condition - clear every target, with rat HP as the budget - rather than retrofitting the nine levels. That is strictly better. Retrofitting would have needed a fail state for running out of targets (because score rewards fewer hits, exhausting the board would otherwise score 4000 on L1 for never touching your rat), and the 3-4 hit pacing leaves a destruction mechanic almost no room to fire. The alternate-win framing also produces the game's first genuinely two-sided trade: with target damage decoupled from self damage, glass clears in few swings but costs a lot of HP while steel is cheap in HP but slow, so neither dominates - which is exactly what tasks 126 and 144 went looking for and could not find. It needs a roughly 6x yoyoDamage spread (2.5/1.0/0.42), contradicting the campaign's <=1.5x guard, so those levels need their OWN material table - which also keeps the nine tuned levels untouched.

decisions.decision: Folded movement zones, a tail-cutting blade obstacle, and general level reorganisation into task 128 rather than filing them separately, and raised 128 to high priority.
decisions.rationale: All three are level-design vocabulary, which is precisely what the 128 design gate exists to decide; filing them as separate implementation items would presume its answer. Three observations attached so the design starts from what is already known rather than rediscovering it. First, a hand constraint has been tried here before - the `hand` px-per-frame knob - and was rejected on 2026-09-11 for capping the skill ceiling without fixing the tunneling it targeted; a positional zone is a different constraint and plausibly has the opposite effect, but the history is relevant. Second, the blade is viable only because task 124's link-level CCD brought rope link crossings under 1%; before that a tail hazard would have killed through contacts the renderer never showed. Third, both the blade and task 151 introduce a fail state into a game that currently has none, so that decision should be made once, here, rather than separately per feature. Also noted: task 149 measured shield placement as dominating shield tier, which is the same lever a movement zone controls directly.

decisions.decision: Task 128 design gate: the nine levels are reorganised around a SPATIAL progression - Act 1 open, Act 2 constrained (movement zones), Act 3 hazardous (blades, and the game's first fail state) - rather than each act introducing a mechanic. Act 2 is built and measured first as a pilot.
decisions.rationale: THE FINDING THAT DECIDED IT: the nine levels are one level with different furniture. Measured across levels.js, the pivot sits at x 0.20-0.24 in ALL nine (a 4% band) and y 0.44-0.50, everything else sits at x 0.48-0.86, and rope length spans only 120-150. Hand on the left at mid-height, stuff on the right, nine times. That single fact explains four things previously treated as unrelated: the flat difficulty curve (act means 3.60/3.68/3.81 hits) because the spatial problem never changes and only furniture varies; the shield-avoiding bot clearing 24/24 runs across L4-L9, because there is always open space to swing into; shield PLACEMENT dominating shield tier in the task 149 measurement, because placement is the only real variable and is barely used; and nothing lasting beyond 3-4 hits, because no arrangement forces a longer engagement. It also means the pivot is an untapped lever that costs no new code - moving it changes the entire spatial problem using what already exists. So each act now poses a different QUESTION rather than introducing a mechanic: can you build and aim speed (open), can you do it in a confined space (constrained), can you do it without getting cut (hazardous). REJECTED: adding zones and blades to the existing levels, which would put two more pieces of furniture in the room whose sameness is the actual problem - the last three balance passes each found that furniture is a weak lever; and rebuilding the level set from scratch, which discards nine levels of tuning and art to fix a problem that is about arrangement rather than content. THE FAIL STATE is settled here, once, rather than separately per feature: Act 3 is where the game becomes losable, via blades, and task 151's alternate-win mode inherits that decision rather than making its own. ACT 2 IS THE PILOT (L0029): it is where zones land and the weakest act today, and the design rests on an untested claim that constraining space produces deliberate play rather than irritation - three levels is a far cheaper place to discover otherwise than nine. Step 4, the human measurement of the pilot, is a real gate on Acts 3 and 1 proceeding at all.

decisions.decision: Task 156 pilot verdict: PROCEED. Constrained space does produce more deliberate play. But the zones broke the shield tier calibration, which needs fixing before Act 3 is re-laid.
decisions.rationale: 19 human runs on the re-laid Act 2 against 28 on the previous layout. THE PREMISE HOLDS: glancing rate fell 27.9% -> 17.3%, a 38% reduction in sloppy hits, against an unchanged Acts 1/3 control in the same export at 22.6% - so it is the zones, not general drift. Time to clear roughly doubled (3.1s -> 5.7s) while hits barely moved (3.5 -> 4.0) and swing speed halved (p50 130.3 -> 69.4): players are landing better hits rather than faster ones, which is what deliberate play looks like. Zero non-SHATTER outcomes across all 19 runs, and yanks stayed at 0, so there is no tangling or abandonment signal. PER LEVEL: Low Ceiling 4 hits / 3.8s / 10% glancing is the cleanest; Narrow Column 4 hits / 6.8s / 27% glancing is the weakest, its constraint producing no accuracy gain; Long Reach 3 hits / 16.1s / 14% glancing is much the slowest, on only 5 runs. THE COUPLED FAILURE, and the reason task 161 exists: halving swing speed halved arrival speed at shields, and the tiers were derived from the OLD layout's arrival distribution. Measured, light fell 56% -> 31% of contacts, medium 30% -> 14%, and heavy 40% -> 2% with only 1 of 5 runs getting through against 57% before. Heavy's highest recorded contact speed is 96.0 against a threshold of 95, so it barely clears at absolute best, and contacts ballooned from 10 to 47 as players bounced off repeatedly. This is the unreachable-180-shield failure returning by another route, and it is L0455 exactly: a threshold measured where the check fires is still invalidated when the level layout moves the distribution underneath it. The structural fix is probably to express a tier RELATIVE to the speed a level actually allows rather than as an absolute px/step, the same move that made parHits per-variant.

decisions.decision: Shield tiers gain a per-level shieldSpeedScale rather than per-level absolute overrides or a geometry-derived scale. The table keeps the relative ordering; the level supplies one number for what it physically permits.
decisions.rationale: An absolute threshold cannot survive a layout change, which the Act 2 pilot proved: zones halved swing speed and therefore arrival speed, and heavy fell from breaking in 57% of runs to 2% of contacts, with a maximum recorded contact speed of 96.0 against its threshold of 95. The measurement also said what kind of fix was needed. Only the SCALE was wrong, not the ordering: zoned levels needed 0.74-0.81x the table across all three tiers and unzoned needed 1.07-1.18x, each group internally consistent, so a single number per level captures it and keeps one pacing dial with a documented ratio (L0409). REJECTED: per-level absolute tier overrides, which is two dials for one thing and lets the relative ordering silently drift between levels; and deriving the scale from geometry, which the data rules out - the widest zone (Low Ceiling, 462px) has the LOWEST swing p50 at 56.4 while the narrowest (Long Reach, 121px) reaches 69.4, so zone dimensions do not predict achievable speed and an automatic derivation would encode a relationship that is not there. ALSO TESTED AND REJECTED: expressing tiers as a fraction of the level's swing speed, which looks elegant and fails, because the fractions differ by group (zoned 0.56/0.86/1.08 vs unzoned 0.41/0.58/0.79) - in a confined space contacts land nearer peak speed, so the shape of the arrival distribution changes rather than just its scale. The old absolute reachability guard was replaced rather than rescaled, since an absolute bound cannot police a per-level scale.

decisions.decision: Task 161 validated and closed: shieldSpeedScale 0.75 restores all three tiers on the zoned levels, and one scale serves all three.
decisions.rationale: Break rates under shieldSpeedScale 0.75, measured on 26 shield-bearing human runs: light 82% of contacts and 100% of runs, medium 58% and 92%, heavy 26% and 75% - against 31/85, 14/67 and 2/20 before. NO TIER NEAR 0%, the ordering holds, and pacing is untouched (hits median 4.0, glancing 17.7%, zero failed runs across 49 zoned runs). ONE SCALE SERVES ALL THREE LEVELS: per level, Low Ceiling light 88%, Narrow Column light 79% / medium 60%, Long Reach medium 57% / heavy 26% - consistently ordered, so per-level scales are not needed. The tiers land easier than the original 99/74/44 design intent, which is logged as task 163 rather than corrected now, because the usable window is narrow: heavy's highest recorded arrival is 91.7 against a 71.25 threshold, so raising the scale to 0.9 would put heavy at 85.5 and back within a few px/step of unreachable. decisions.rationale: Two independent causes: there was no ceiling at all, and 50px side walls against a documented ~50 px/step tunnelling threshold with measured rat peaks of 250-460 px/step. Thicker static geometry costs nothing per step and adds no code path, where extending the swept collision would have touched the body that carries the damage - which the 2026-09-11 decision excluded on purpose. Accepted behaviour change: the rat now rebounds off the top rather than leaving. THE TESTING LESSON IS THE DURABLE PART. The obvious check - whip the hand at the boundaries and watch the rat - was written first and PASSED with the ceiling deliberately removed, because the escape reproduced in a run of 90 iterations and the check ran 80. A containment test that can pass while containment is absent is worse than no test, since it manufactures confidence. The structural assertion (the bodies exist and exceed a thickness floor) is deterministic, was verified to fail with the ceiling removed, and the behavioural whip is kept only as an INFO line alongside the HP-drop report.
